title: Do Satanic Pedophiles Really Run the World?
dek: One in five Americans told pollsters yes. We traced the story from the 1980s daycare panic to Pizzagate, Q and the Epstein files. Here's what's real and what isn't.
body: Short answer: no. Long answer: no, but the reasons people believe it are worth understanding, because this story has already put a gun in a pizza place and it keeps coming back like a horror franchise.

The pitch goes like this: a secret ring of Satan-worshipping elites, politicians, Hollywood stars and bankers, abuses children and secretly runs the world. In a March 2022 survey by the Public Religion Research Institute, 18 percent of Americans agreed that the government, media and financial worlds are controlled by Satan-worshipping pedophiles. Nearly one in five. So let's look at it.

This plot is older than the internet. In the 1980s, America convinced itself that secret satanic cults were abusing kids in daycares. The biggest case, the McMartin preschool trial in California, dragged on for years in the late '80s and ended with no convictions. In 1992 the FBI's own expert on crimes against children, Kenneth Lanning, published a report saying the bureau had found no evidence that organized satanic ritual abuse cults existed. Lives were ruined anyway.

In 2016, a theory spread online that a child-abuse ring was operating out of the basement of a Washington, D.C., pizza place called Comet Ping Pong. The restaurant doesn't have a basement. That December, a man drove up from North Carolina and fired a rifle inside to 'self-investigate.' Nobody was hurt, he found nothing, and he went to prison.
> The restaurant doesn't have a basement.

In October 2017, an anonymous poster calling himself 'Q' started dropping cryptic 'intel' on 4chan, promising that a secret war against the cabal was about to end in mass arrests. It never happened. The predictions kept failing and the story kept stretching to cover the misses. It spread through Facebook groups, YouTube and eventually into political rallies, and by 2020 it had people convinced a furniture website was selling children inside overpriced cabinets. It wasn't.

Here's why the theory sticks: some powerful men really did abuse kids and young women. Jeffrey Epstein was a convicted sex offender with famous friends who died in jail in 2019 awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges. His associate Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted in 2021. That's documented, prosecuted and real.

After years of public pressure, Congress passed a law in November 2025 forcing the Justice Department to release its Epstein files. The final batch came out January 30, 2026: more than 3 million pages, 2,000 videos and 180,000 images, heavily redacted to protect victims. The deputy attorney general denied the department was covering for Epstein's associates. What the files did not reveal was a satanic cabal running the planet. They revealed something more ordinary and more damning: rich, connected people who looked away, and a justice system that went easy on a rich man for years.

If you care about protecting kids, and everybody should, the cabal story points you in exactly the wrong direction. Most child sexual abuse is committed by someone the child already knows: a relative, a family friend, a coach, a trusted adult. Not a hooded billionaire. Every hour spent decoding Q drops is an hour not spent noticing what's happening in your own family, church or school.
Conspiracy theories also make it harder for real victims to be believed. When everything is a cabal, real abuse gets lost in the noise, and real investigators get buried in junk tips.

Do satanic pedophiles run the world? No. Do powerful people sometimes get away with terrible things? Absolutely, and that's worth being furious about. Get furious at the real ones, with real evidence, in real courts.

If you think a child is being hurt, don't post about it. Report it. In the U.S., call the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 1-800-422-4453, or report online exploitation to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children's CyberTipline. If a child is in immediate danger, call 911.
